passages.happening:
‘Now King Xerxes imposed tribute throughout the land, even to its farthest shores’ (verse 1). The full account of his power, and of the greatness to which he raised Mordecai, is written, the book says, ‘in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia’ (verse 2).

The book ends with Mordecai: ‘For Mordecai the Jew was second only to King Xerxes, preeminent among the Jews and highly favored by his many kinsmen, seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his countrymen’ (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The epilogue is short and formal, like the closing notices of the kings' reigns in the books of Kings. It frames the whole book. Chapter 1 opened with Xerxes' power and splendor, and chapter 10 returns to his power, but it ends with Mordecai.

Tribute from subject peoples was the financial backbone of the Persian state. The reliefs at Persepolis show delegations from many nations bringing gifts to the king.

The Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia has not survived. A clay tablet from about the time of Xerxes mentions an official named Marduka serving at Susa, and the name appears in other Persian records, but whether any of these refers to the Mordecai of this book cannot be shown.

To be second to the king was a known office in ancient empires. Joseph held such a post under Pharaoh, and Daniel was raised high under Babylonian and Persian kings. Mordecai joins the Jews who served foreign kings faithfully without giving up who they were. And the last words describe a good leader as Israel's tradition understood one: not seeking his own advancement but the good of his people, and speaking peace, shalom, to them all.
passages.later: The closing formula is the one the books of Kings use for Israel's rulers. Of the rest of Solomon's acts it asks, ‘are they not written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon?’ (1 Kings 11:41). And Joseph, too, was second to a foreign king: ‘Only with regard to the throne will I be greater than you’ (Genesis 41:40).
passages.asks: The book ends with a powerful man using his power for the good of his people and to speak peace. Ask what power or influence you hold, however small, and whose good it serves. And ask to whom you could speak peace this week.
